Let \(g\geq2\) be an integer, and set
\[
r=\left\lfloor\frac{g+2}{3}\right\rfloor,\qquad k=g-r.
\]
Let \(C_g\) be the smooth projective completion over \(\mathbb C\) of the affine curve
\[
z^2=x^{2g+1}-1,
\]
and let \(p\) be its unique point over infinity. Choose the local parameter \(t\) at \(p\) satisfying
\[
x=t^{-2},\qquad z=t^{-(2g+1)}(1-t^{4g+2})^{1/2},
\]
where the square root has value \(1\) at \(t=0\).

For a nonzero vector \(b=(b_0,\ldots,b_{r-1})\in\mathbb C^r\), define
\[
\phi_b(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}b_jt^{-(2g-1-2j)}.
\]
Choose coordinate discs \(W_0\Subset W\) centered at \(p\), with \(t\) defined on a neighborhood of \(\overline W\), and put \(U=C_g\setminus\overline{W_0}\). Take product neighborhoods of the zero sections over \(U\) and \(W\), with fiber coordinates \(y_U\) and \(y_W\). After shrinking the fiber directions, glue them over \(U\cap W\), preserving the base point, by
\[
y_W=t^{-1}y_U\bigl(1+k\phi_b(t)y_U^k\bigr)^{-1/k}.
\]
The fractional power denotes the holomorphic branch whose value is \(1\) at \(y_U=0\).

Let \(X_b\) be the resulting smooth analytic surface germ along its zero section \(E\simeq C_g\). Its normal bundle is \(\mathcal O_{C_g}(-p)\), and contracting \(E\) gives a normal surface singularity \((V_b,0)\) with minimal good resolution \(f_b:(X_b,E)\to(V_b,0)\). For cohomology, take \(X_b\) to be the inverse image of a sufficiently small Stein representative of this singularity.

Write \(\mathcal I_E\) for the ideal sheaf of \(E\), and define the logarithmic tangent sheaf by
\[
S_b=\{D\in\Theta_{X_b}:D(\mathcal I_E)\subseteq\mathcal I_E\},
\]
where \(\Theta_{X_b}\) is the sheaf of holomorphic vector fields. Put \(L_b=\bigwedge^2S_b\) and \(h^1(X_b,\mathcal F)=\dim_{\mathbb C}H^1(X_b,\mathcal F)\). Determine the exact formula, as a function of \(g\) and the entire coefficient vector \(b\), for
\[
\Delta_b=h^1(X_b,\mathcal O_{X_b})-h^1(X_b,S_b)+h^1(X_b,L_b),
\]
for every allowed nonzero \(b\), including vectors with vanishing components.
</problem>

192	### 2.3. Uniform bounds on poles

239	### 2.4. A finite principal-parts calculation

241	The sequence
242	\[
243	0\longrightarrow F_N\longrightarrow F_N(Mp)
244	 \longrightarrow F_N(Mp)/F_N\longrightarrow0

246	and (16) imply
247	\[
248	h^1(F_N)=dM-
249	\operatorname{rank}\!\left(
250	H^0(F_N(Mp))\longrightarrow H^0(F_N(Mp)/F_N)
251	\right).                                                 \tag{17}
252	\]
253	
254	By (15), a section of \(F_N(Mp)\), expressed in the frame off \(p\), is a vector of meromorphic functions having poles only at \(p\), of orders at most \(K=M+D\).
255	
256	The affine coordinate ring of \(C_g\setminus\{p\}\) is
257	\[
258	\mathbb C[x,z]/(z^2-x^{2g+1}+1).
259	\]
260	The pole orders of \(x,z\) are \(2,2g+1\). Thus a basis of
261	\(H^0(C_g,\mathcal O(Kp))\) is exactly
262	\[
263	x^{m/2}\quad(m\text{ even}),\qquad
264	x^{(m-2g-1)/2}z\quad(m\text{ odd},\ m\ge2g+1),
265	\]
266	with \(m\le K\). Their Laurent expansions are the \(a_{m,\epsilon}\) used in (4).
267	
268	Transforming a vector in this basis to the frame at \(p\) gives \(A_F\). No exponent below \(-P=-(K+D)\) can occur, by (13).
269	
270	Such a vector is a section of \(F_N(Mp)\) exactly when its coefficients of \(t^e\), \(e<-M\), vanish. Its coordinate vector therefore belongs to \(\ker B_F\). Its principal part modulo \(F_N\) consists of the coefficients with \(-M\le e<0\).

272	If \(C_F\) denotes these remaining rows, elementary linear algebra gives
273	\[
274	\operatorname{rank}(C_F|_{\ker B_F})
275	 =\operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}B_F\\C_F\end{pmatrix}
276	  -\operatorname{rank}B_F
277	 =\operatorname{rank}A_F-\operatorname{rank}B_F.
278	\]
279	Substitution into (17), followed by (9), proves
280	\[
281	h^1(X_b,F)=dM-\operatorname{rank}A_F+\operatorname{rank}B_F.
282	                                                                    \tag{18}
283	\]
284	The terms \(dM\) cancel in the combination \(O-S+L\), since
285	\(N-2N+N=0\). Equation (18) is therefore exactly (6).

287	This proof made no nonvanishing or genericity assumption about any coefficient.

117	## 2. Proof
118	
119	### 2.1. Reduction to a finite infinitesimal neighborhood
120	
121	The gluing preserves the base, so there is a retraction
122	\[
123	\pi:X_b\longrightarrow C_g.
124	\]
125	For \(F=\mathcal O_{X_b},S_b,L_b\), write
126	\[
127	F_N=F/\mathcal I_E^NF.
128	\]
129	Through \(\pi\), these are vector bundles on \(C_g\), of ranks \(N,2N,N\), respectively.
130	
131	We first prove that
132	\[
133	H^1(X_b,F)\simeq H^1(C_g,F_N).                             \tag{9}
134	\]
135	
136	The associated graded pieces of \(\mathcal O_{X_b}\) are
137	\[
138	\mathcal I_E^n/\mathcal I_E^{n+1}\simeq\mathcal O_{C_g}(np).
139	\]
140	Moreover,
141	\[
142	0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{C_g}
143	 \longrightarrow S_b|_E
144	 \longrightarrow T_{C_g}\longrightarrow0,
145	\qquad
146	L_b|_E\simeq T_{C_g}.
147	\]
148	Consequently, the graded pieces for \(S_b\) are extensions of
149	\(\mathcal O(np)\) and \(T_{C_g}(np)\), and those for \(L_b\) are
150	\(T_{C_g}(np)\).
151	
152	If \(n\ge N=4g-3\), both line bundles have vanishing \(H^1\): their degrees exceed \(2g-2\). The exact sequences for successive infinitesimal neighborhoods therefore show that their first cohomology stabilizes at \(N\).
153	
154	Finally, apply the theorem on formal functions to the proper resolution over a sufficiently small Stein representative. The higher direct images in question are supported at the singular point and have finite length. The maximal-ideal-adic and \(E\)-adic topologies are cofinal. Thus the stabilized infinitesimal cohomology equals \(H^1(X_b,F)\), proving (9).
155	
156	### 2.2. Computing the three transition matrices
157	
158	On \(C_g\setminus\{p\}\), the vector field
159	\[
160	V=2z\,\partial_x+(2g+1)x^{2g}\,\partial_z
161	\]
162	is a nowhere-vanishing frame of the tangent bundle. At \(p\),
163	\[
164	V=v(t)\partial_t,\qquad
165	v(t)=-t^{2-2g}(1-t^{4g+2})^{1/2}.                          \tag{10}
166	\]
167	
168	Write \(u=y_U\) and \(q=y_W\). Inverting the specified gluing gives
169	\[
170	u=tq(1-kt^k\phi_bq^k)^{-1/k}=tqB^{-1/k}.                  \tag{11}
171	\]
172	In particular, \(u^n=Q_n\).
173	
174	For \(S_b\), use frames
175	\[
176	(V,u\partial_u)\quad\text{and}\quad(\partial_t,q\partial_q).
177	\]
178	Direct differentiation of the gluing gives
179	\[
180	u\partial_u=Bq\partial_q,
181	\]
182	and
183	\[
184	V=
185	v\partial_t-v\bigl(t^{-1}+t^k\phi_b' q^k\bigr)q\partial_q.
186	                                                                    \tag{12}
187	\]
188	Multiplying (12) by \(u^n\), and reducing modulo \(q^N\), gives precisely (3). Taking determinants gives the stated matrix \(T_L\). The matrix \(T_O\) follows immediately from (11).
189	
190	### 2.3. Uniform bounds on poles
191	
192	We need the following bound, valid also when some \(b_j\) vanish:
193	\[
194	t^DT_F,\quad t^DT_F^{-1}\quad\text{are holomorphic at }t=0. \tag{13}
195	\]
196	
197	Here are explicit inverse formulas, which also verify this assertion. Put
198	\[
199	H=1+k\phi_b(t)u^k,\qquad
200	\widehat Q_n=t^{-n}u^nH^{-n/k},\qquad
201	\widehat R_n=t^{-n}u^nH^{1-n/k}.
202	\]
203	Modulo \(u^N\), the inverse columns are
204	\[
205	\begin{array}{c|c}
206	F&\text{inverse columns}\\ \hline
207	O&\widehat Q_n\\[2mm]
208	L&v^{-1}\widehat R_n\\[2mm]
209	S&
210	\displaystyle
211	\begin{pmatrix}
212	v^{-1}\widehat Q_n\\
213	t^{-1}\widehat R_n+\phi_b'u^k\widehat Q_n
214	\end{pmatrix},
215	\quad
216	\begin{pmatrix}0\\\widehat R_n\end{pmatrix}.
217	\end{array}                                               \tag{14}
218	\]
219	
220	In a term surviving modulo \(u^N\) or \(q^N\), at most \(J\) factors of \(\phi_b\) occur. The pole order of \(\phi_b\) is at most \(2g-1\), while that of \(\phi_b'\) is at most \(2g\). In (14), including the possible derivative term, the pole order is therefore at most
221	\[
222	N+J(2g-1)=D.
223	\]
224	For the forward matrices, the factors \(t^k\) improve this estimate; the same bound \(D\) holds. The factors \(s,s^{-1}\) are holomorphic units. This proves (13).
225	
226	Regard \(F_N\) as a meromorphic modification of the trivial bundle using its frame off \(p\). Bound (13) says
227	\[
228	\mathcal O_{C_g}(-Dp)^d
229	 \ \subseteq\ F_N\ \subseteq\
230	\mathcal O_{C_g}(Dp)^d.                                   \tag{15}
231	\]
232	Because \(M-D=2g-1>2g-2\), the left inclusion, twisted by \(Mp\), gives
233	\[
234	H^1(C_g,F_N(Mp))=0.                                       \tag{16}
235	\]
236	
237	### 2.4. A finite principal-parts calculation
238	
239	The sequence
240	\[
241	0\longrightarrow F_N\longrightarrow F_N(Mp)
242	 \longrightarrow F_N(Mp)/F_N\longrightarrow0
243	\]
244	and (16) imply
245	\[
246	h^1(F_N)=dM-
247	\operatorname{rank}\!\left(
248	H^0(F_N(Mp))\longrightarrow H^0(F_N(Mp)/F_N)
249	\right).                                                 \tag{17}
250	\]
251	
252	By (15), a section of \(F_N(Mp)\), expressed in the frame off \(p\), is a vector of meromorphic functions having poles only at \(p\), of orders at most \(K=M+D\).
253	
254	The affine coordinate ring of \(C_g\setminus\{p\}\) is
255	\[
256	\mathbb C[x,z]/(z^2-x^{2g+1}+1).
257	\]
258	The pole orders of \(x,z\) are \(2,2g+1\). Thus a basis of
259	\(H^0(C_g,\mathcal O(Kp))\) is exactly
260	\[
261	x^{m/2}\quad(m\text{ even}),\qquad
262	x^{(m-2g-1)/2}z\quad(m\text{ odd},\ m\ge2g+1),
263	\]
264	with \(m\le K\). Their Laurent expansions are the \(a_{m,\epsilon}\) used in (4).
265	
266	Transforming a vector in this basis to the frame at \(p\) gives \(A_F\). No exponent below \(-P=-(K+D)\) can occur, by (13).
267	
268	Such a vector is a section of \(F_N(Mp)\) exactly when its coefficients of \(t^e\), \(e<-M\), vanish. Its coordinate vector therefore belongs to \(\ker B_F\). Its principal part modulo \(F_N\) consists of the coefficients with \(-M\le e<0\).
269	
270	If \(C_F\) denotes these remaining rows, elementary linear algebra gives
271	\[
272	\operatorname{rank}(C_F|_{\ker B_F})
273	 =\operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}B_F\\C_F\end{pmatrix}
274	  -\operatorname{rank}B_F
275	 =\operatorname{rank}A_F-\operatorname{rank}B_F.
276	\]
277	Substitution into (17), followed by (9), proves
278	\[
279	h^1(X_b,F)=dM-\operatorname{rank}A_F+\operatorname{rank}B_F.
280	                                                                    \tag{18}
281	\]
282	The terms \(dM\) cancel in the combination \(O-S+L\), since
283	\(N-2N+N=0\). Equation (18) is therefore exactly (6).
284	
285	This proof made no nonvanishing or genericity assumption about any coefficient.
